_about: Craft terms explained, each anchored in four Tamil films the Studio already teaches from. Definitions and examples are original analysis — no plot text or dialogue is reproduced from the films. `tanglish` mirrors the English gloss the way the blueprints already do. Terms are matched case-insensitively against step prose by autoTagGlossary() in src/ui/chrome.js; `aliases` catch the inflections that appear in the copy. `stage` files each term under Story, Screenplay, Pre-production, Production or Post (story|screenplay|preprod|production|post) for the library's Film terminology space. `seeAlso` names other terms. `notag: true` keeps an everyday word (take, wrap, scene) out of the automatic popover tagging while leaving it in the library and in search.

terms.def: One sentence carrying the protagonist, their want, the obstacle, and the cost of failure. If it needs a second sentence, the story is not yet decided.
terms.tanglish: Oru vaakkiyathula padam. Hero yaaru, enna venum, edhu thadukkudhu, thotta enna nashtam.

examples.note: A college dropout buys a fake degree to land a corporate job, and must clear 48 real arrears in three months when the one man who knows recognises him.
A fearful rookie officer must out-think a serial killer before his own nerve, not the case, defeats him.
Two people who loved each other at sixteen get one night, twenty-two years later, to say what they never said.
An encounter cop hunting a gangster is handed three stories that make his own certainty unusable.

terms.def: What is actually lost if the protagonist fails. Stakes must be specific and personal — 'the city is in danger' is a premise, not a stake.
terms.tanglish: Thotta enna poidum. Podhuvaa 'ooru azhiyum' illa — ivanukku personal-aa enna poidum.

examples.note: Exposure costs him the job, the engagement, and his father's belief — three separate losses, each with a face attached.
Nothing external is at risk at all. The stake is that the thing unsaid at sixteen stays unsaid forever. Proof that internal stakes carry a whole film.
The next victim is the public stake; the private one is whether the rookie stays a man who runs.
What is at risk is not the cop's life but his right to believe he is the good one.

terms.def: The argument the film makes, not the topic it covers. State it as a sentence someone could disagree with.
terms.tanglish: Padam enna vaadhaadudhu. Subject illa — oru statement, yaaraavadhu maruththu pesa mudiyanum.

examples.note: A shortcut is a debt, and it is collected with interest from people who did not take it.
Some loves are complete precisely because they were never consummated.
Courage is not the absence of fear but the decision to keep looking.
Good and evil are positions, and position depends on where you are standing.

terms.def: The conscious, stateable goal the protagonist would name if asked. It drives the plot. It is usually the wrong thing.
terms.tanglish: Avanukku theriyura aasai. Kepta sollum goal. Adhu porumbaaluma thappaana vishayam.

examples.note: A salary big enough to outrank his ex-girlfriend's fiancé. He can say it out loud, and it is entirely about being seen.
One more evening in the same room. Small, sayable, and not actually what he is missing.
To close the case — a want handed to him by rank rather than chosen.
To find and finish Vedha, cleanly, the way the previous encounters went.

terms.def: What the protagonist must accept to be whole, usually unknown to them and often the opposite of the want. The arc is the distance between the two.
terms.tanglish: Avanukku theriyaama theva-padra vishayam. Want-ukku ethir-maari irukkum. Arc-nu solradhu inda rendukkum edaila ulla dooram.

examples.note: Self-respect he did not fake. He gets it only after confessing and serving the sentence — the want (status) is destroyed to reach it.
To let the memory be enough. The want (more time) is refused, and the need is met anyway.
To stop outsourcing his nerve to the senior officer standing next to him.
To admit that his certainty was a convenience, not a moral position.

terms.def: The false belief about themselves or the world that the protagonist carries at page one. The story exists to test it.
terms.tanglish: Modhal page-la character nambura poi. Kadhai adha odaikkardhukku thaan irukku.

examples.note: 'The result is what counts; how I got it is nobody's business.' The film spends its whole second half billing him for that sentence.
'If I do not touch it, it stays perfect.' True and ruinous at the same time — the film never quite calls it a lie.
'I am not built for this work.' Held so firmly it nearly becomes true.
'I only shoot the guilty, so I am clean.'

terms.def: The event that makes the old normal unavailable. Not the first dramatic thing that happens — the first thing the protagonist cannot ignore.
terms.tanglish: Pazhaya normal-a thirumba mudiyaadha padi maathura event. Modhal drama illa — avanaala ignore panna mudiyaadha modhal vishayam.

examples.note: The dean recognises him. Everything before that is setup; from here the clock and the blackmail exist.
The reunion invitation. Trivial on paper, and it reopens twenty-two years.
The posting itself — the rookie is placed beside the one man who will not let him look away.
Vedha walks into the station and surrenders, choosing the terms of his own capture.

terms.def: The measurable change in what a character believes, shown through choices rather than stated. Write the first and last decision; the arc is the line between them.
terms.tanglish: Character-oda nambikkai maaradhu, dialogue-la sollaama choice-la kaatta-num. Modhal decision, kadaisi decision — adhukku naduvula thaan arc.

examples.note: First decision: buy the degree. Last decision: confess to four separate people with nothing left to gain. Same man, inverted.
Textbook positive arc — the trainee who flinches becomes the one who makes the deduction that closes the case.
A deliberate flat arc. Neither changes, and the film is about discovering they did not need to.
The cop's certainty erodes in three stages, one per story told to him.

terms.def: A detail placed early so a later payoff feels earned rather than convenient. A good setup has its own reason to be in the scene.
terms.tanglish: Munnadiye vechu, appuram use panna detail. Nalla setup-ku andha scene-la thaniyaa oru reason irukkum.

examples.note: The odd reverse-gear sound, dropped inside a confession about something else entirely. It is a character detail first and a clue second — which is why it does not announce itself.
The 48 arrears are a running joke long before they become the mechanism of the plot.
Photographs, established as his profession, become the film's method of holding time.
The folk-tale frame is stated up front, so the structure itself is the setup.

terms.def: The later moment a setup pays for. The audience should feel they could have seen it coming and did not.
terms.tanglish: Setup panna vishayam palan tharura edam. Paarthavanga 'ithu munnadiye irundhuchey' nu unara-num, aana andha nerathula theriyakoodaadhu.

examples.note: That reverse-gear sound identifies the vehicle and the killer. The clue was always audible; the film simply refused to point at it.
The arrears he treated as a joke become the exact measure of the debt he has to clear.
Each folk tale pays off as a moral trap the cop has already walked into.
The song withheld for most of the film finally arrives, and carries everything unspoken with it.

terms.def: The centre turn where the protagonist stops reacting and starts acting, usually on new information that reframes the problem.
terms.tanglish: Nadu-la varura thirupam. Ithu varaikkum react panninavan, ippo thaane move edukka aarambikaraan.

examples.note: He stops dodging the dean and commits to actually clearing the arrears — the goal shifts from hiding to doing.
The prime suspect turns out to be a teacher of the method, not its user. The case the team was solving no longer exists.
The second tale lands and the cop begins interrogating his own record instead of the gangster.
The reunion ends and the night becomes private. The film changes from group nostalgia to two people.

terms.def: Anything standing between the protagonist and the want. The best obstacles are people with their own defensible reasons.
terms.tanglish: Hero-kum avan aasaikkum naduvula nikkura edhuvum. Nalla obstacle-nu solradhu — sariyaana karanam vechirukkura oru manushan.

examples.note: The dean is not a villain. He is a man enforcing a rule that is entirely correct, which is what makes him immovable.
The obstacle is a marriage nobody in the film treats as an enemy, and the characters' own decency.
The rookie's own fear obstructs him more often than the killer does.
The obstacle is an argument, not a man — Vedha's questions, which cannot be shot.

terms.def: What the scene is about while the characters discuss something else. If the dialogue states the feeling, the subtext has been deleted.
terms.tanglish: Pesaradhu onnu, scene-oda artham innonnu. Feeling-a dialogue-la nerada sonna, subtext poidum.

examples.note: Almost the entire film. Two people discuss school, food, and a song, and never once state the thing the scene is about.
Each folk tale is a confession disguised as a riddle.
The banter with his friends keeps circling money and worth without either word being the subject.
The senior officer's instruction is always procedural on the surface and always about the junior's nerve underneath.

terms.def: Information the audience needs. The craft is not avoiding it but hiding it inside conflict, so it arrives while attention is elsewhere.
terms.tanglish: Paarvaiyaalarukku theriya vendiya thagaval. Thavirkuradhu illa — conflict-ukkulla olichu kudukkuradhu thaan vidhai.

examples.note: Procedure is explained to the trainee, so the audience learns the rules while a character is being tested on them.
Backstory is delivered as three tales the antagonist chooses to tell — exposition becomes an act of aggression.
The arrears count is repeated as comedy long before it has to be understood as arithmetic.
Twenty-two missing years are conveyed by what the two avoid asking.

terms.def: The moment the protagonist makes the choice the whole film has been arranging. It answers the theme, not just the plot.
terms.tanglish: Padam muzhusaa thayaar panna andha choice-a hero edukkura edam. Plot-ukku mattum illa, theme-ukkum badhil.

examples.note: The confession. He is not caught — he chooses the loss, which is the only move that answers the theme.
The rookie makes the deduction alone. The case closes because the arc completed, not the other way round.
The parting. Refusing the want is the climax.
The cop has to answer the last question himself, with no third story coming to save him.

terms.def: New information that reorganises everything already seen. A twist that only surprises is a trick; a reveal makes the earlier scenes mean more on a second watch.
terms.tanglish: Munnadi paartha ellathaiyum maathi amaikkura pudhu thagaval. Suma shock kudukkuradhu trick — nalla reveal, rendaam murai paakkumbodhu scene-ellam perusaa theriyum.

examples.note: The suspect is a killer, just not this one — he taught the method. Every interrogation scene before it changes meaning.
The classmate's ruined life lands as a reveal about the protagonist rather than the plot: the cost was always being paid by someone else.
Each tale reveals that the cop is already inside the story he is being told.
The film withholds almost nothing factually, and still reveals — what changes is what the audience understands the silence to mean.

terms.def: The character whose choices drive the story and whose belief is tested. Not necessarily the most screen time — the one who changes, or refuses to.
terms.tanglish: Yaaroda choice kadhaiya nagarthudho, yaaroda nambikkai test aagudho avan thaan. Screen time mukkiyam illa.

examples.note: Ragavan. Every plot turn is caused by a decision he made, including the ones that destroy him.
The trainee, not the senior officer — the film belongs to whoever is being changed by it.
Shared almost equally, which is rare and a deliberate structural risk.
The cop, even though the gangster has the better lines and controls the telling.

terms.def: The force opposing the want. Strongest when it is a person with a coherent philosophy rather than a person with bad intentions.
terms.tanglish: Hero-oda aasaiku ethiraana sakthi. Ketta ennam ulla aal illa — sariyaana logic vechirukkuravan thaan strong antagonist.

examples.note: The purest example here: the antagonist's position is arguable, and the film lets him argue it.
The dean opposes him with nothing but a correct rule, which is harder to fight than malice.
A killer with a private and coherent logic, which is exactly what makes him findable.
No antagonist at all — time is the opposition. Worth studying for how a film holds without one.

terms.def: The line that opens a scene: interior or exterior, where, and what time of day. It is not decoration — it is the unit the whole schedule is built from, because every department reads it to work out what a day costs.
terms.tanglish: Scene oda mudhal line — INT/EXT, edam, neram. Idhu vechu thaan schedule-um budget-um decide aagum.

examples.note: Time of day is doing the structural work: the same place at a different hour is a different scene with a different meaning, and the heading is where that turn is declared.
Interiors dominate, and the headings show it — a procedural gains pressure by refusing to go outside, and the slug list is where that choice becomes visible before a frame is shot.
A handful of locations recur under many headings. Repetition in the slug list is not poverty of invention; it is how a film makes a place feel inescapable.
Headings alternate between two worlds on a rhythm. Read the slug list alone and the film's structure is already legible.

terms.def: An edit that joins two shots by a shared shape, movement or sound, so the cut reads as a rhyme rather than a break. It makes a comparison the dialogue never has to state.
terms.tanglish: Rendu shot-ah ore maadhiri shape illa sound vechu join panradhu. Cut-e oru comparison aagidum, dialogue la sollave vendaam.

examples.note: Cuts across time rhyme on posture and framing, so two decades read as one continuous person rather than a flashback bolted on.
Sound carries across cuts more than image does; an edit joined on a noise keeps the dread continuous while the location changes.
Rhyming cuts are used for comedy first and consequence later — the same visual joke returns once it has stopped being funny.
The film rhymes its two protagonists by cutting on matched actions, arguing they are the same man before the script says so.

terms.def: The smallest unit of change. A scene is made of beats, and a beat ends when something turns — a decision, a refusal, a piece of information that cannot be taken back. A scene with no beat is a scene with no reason to exist.
terms.tanglish: Sinna maatram. Oru scene la edhachum thirumbina, adhu oru beat. Beat illana andha scene-ku velaye illa.

examples.note: Beats are small enough to be almost invisible — a question not answered, a glance held a moment too long — which is why the film can run on conversation alone.
Each beat hands the protagonist a piece of information that raises what he stands to lose, so the investigation and the character test advance on the same move.
Beats turn on arithmetic: every scene changes a number the protagonist is trying not to look at.
The beats are staged as questions put to the other man, so each turn advances the argument and the plot in the same line.

terms.def: The first spark of a film: a situation, a person or a question you cannot stop thinking about. It is not yet a story; it becomes one when you can say who wants what and what stands in the way.
terms.tanglish: Padam-oda modhal porigai. Oru situation, oru aal, illa oru kelvi. Yaar-ku enna venum, edhu thadukkudhu-nu sollum bodhu thaan adhu kadhai aagum.

examples.note: A young man talks his way into a corporate job on a forged degree and is recognised. One situation with a clock already inside it.
Two classmates, one reunion night, twenty-two years apart. The idea is a single evening with a question hanging over it.
A frightened rookie is paired with an unforgiving veteran on a murder case. The idea holds two problems at once: the crime and his nerve.
A cop hunts a gangster who answers only with stories. The idea is a hunt that turns into an argument.

terms.def: One working document that holds the decisions of your story: premise, characters, world, rules and arc. You read it before writing so every scene stays consistent with the rest.
terms.tanglish: Kadhai-oda ella mudivum oru idathula: premise, characters, ulagam, rules. Ezhudhum bodhu ithaye paarthu ezhudhanum.

examples.note: Its bible would pin down the forged degree, the count of unfinished papers and the dean's rule, because the plot is arithmetic that must never contradict itself.
A bible would fix who left when and what each person never said, so the reunion night stays consistent from the first line to the last.
It would hold the killer's fixed pattern, since the investigation only works if the method never changes between one scene and the next.
It would list the three stories and how each shifts the cop's certainty, because the structure is announced in advance and must hold.

terms.def: A short portrait of a person in your story: who they are, what they want, what they fear and what flaw holds them back. Enough to predict what they would do in a scene you have not written.
terms.tanglish: Oru character yaaru-nu sinnadhaa ezhudhi vaikkradhu: enna venum, edhukku bayam, enna kuraai. Ezhudhaadha scene-la avan enna pannuvaan-nu sollidanum.

examples.note: Ragavan is persuasive and believes results are the only thing anybody audits. That profile explains why he buys a shortcut.
Ram is restrained to the point of silence; Janaki is warm but will not pretend. Two profiles that make one quiet night tense.
Prakash is capable on paper and unsteady in the room; Loganathan is armoured by detachment. Opposite profiles on one case.
Vikram trusts a clean record as proof of a clean conscience. His profile is exactly what the film puts to the test.

terms.def: The characters around the protagonist who each press on one side of them: a mirror, an ally, an obstacle. Each should exist for a reason the story needs.
terms.tanglish: Hero-va sutthi irukkura characters. Ovvoruthar-um hero-oda oru pakkatha test pannanum, summa irukka koodaadhu.

examples.note: The classmate is a mirror who prices the protagonist's choice. They stay static on purpose, so the cost is easy to read.
Janaki is the mirror: she holds the other half of the question, so the protagonist cannot answer it alone.
Loganathan states the rules of the work aloud, so procedure becomes a continuous examination of the rookie.
Priya is the control group: she already holds the position the protagonist claims to hold, and the gap is the argument.

terms.def: The wrong belief or habit that keeps a character from what they need. The best flaws feel like strengths to the person who has them.
terms.tanglish: Character-ku thevaiyaanadhu kidaikkaama thadukkura thappaana nambikkai. Nalla flaw-a avan strength-nu nenaippaan.

examples.note: Ragavan believes the result is the only thing anybody audits, so he buys the outcome instead of earning it.
Ram mistakes restraint for integrity: he will not ask for anything he is not offered.
Prakash treats his fear as a verdict on what he is, rather than a condition he is in.
Vikram confuses a clean record with a clean conscience.

terms.def: What a character most dreads facing or losing. It drives their choices, usually in ways they would not admit out loud.
terms.tanglish: Character edhukku romba payapadraan. Adhu thaan avan mudivugalai odikkum, aana avan othukka maattaan.

examples.note: Ragavan wants status the people who wrote him off cannot ignore, which points to a fear of being written off again.
Ram never asks for what he wants unless it is offered, which points to a fear of asking and being refused.
Prakash fears his own nerve failing in the room, and the film never lets a later scene forgive the flinch.
Vikram fears finding out his certainty was a convenience rather than a moral position.

terms.def: A past hurt that shaped the character's flaw and their lie. It usually sits before page one and is revealed late, if at all.
terms.tanglish: Pazhaya kaayam, adhu thaan flaw-um poi-um uruvaakkudhu. Modhal page-ku munnaadiye irukkum, kadaisila thaan therium.

examples.note: Being written off is the wound that explains why the protagonist buys the outcome instead of earning it.
Twenty-two years of things unsaid are the wound the reunion presses on.
The film shows the habit, a flinch in the room, before it explains anything about where it came from.
The pressure here comes from outside: three stories erode his certainty in stages instead of one old injury.

terms.def: The struggle between what a character wants and what stands in their way: another person, the world, or themselves. Without it a scene has nothing to decide.
terms.tanglish: Avan aasaikkum, avanai thadukkuradhukkum naduvula nadakkura mothal. Idhu illaama scene-la mudivu edukka onnum irukkaadhu.

examples.note: The debt is real and the clock is short, and every day spent paying it is a day the invented life can collapse on its own.
Both have lived twenty-two years that cannot be undone, and neither will say so directly.
Every step of the procedure demands exactly the composure the rookie does not have.
The antagonist opposes him with an argument rather than force, and an argument cannot be shot.

terms.def: Where and when the story happens and the rules that hold there: its places, customs and limits. A clear world makes choices feel real.
terms.tanglish: Kadhai nadakkura idam, kaalam, adhula irukkura rules. Ulagam theliva irundha choice nijamaa theriyum.

examples.note: A college and a corporate job joined by one forged document. The dean enforces the rule that holds the whole world together.
A school reunion: a small, closed world in which one evening is the whole clock.
A police investigation whose procedure is stated aloud, so the rules of the world double as exposition.
An encounter cop's world where his method is routine and sanctioned, which the film then puts on trial.

terms.def: A list of the story's key turns in order, such as opening, inciting incident, midpoint and climax. It is a map of what changes, not a plan of every scene.
terms.tanglish: Kadhaila mukkiya thirupangal varisaiyaa. Ovvoru scene-um illa. Enna maarudhu-nu oru map.

examples.note: The opening plays as comedy with a fluent bluffer. The inciting beat is recognition, which starts the clock.
The beats are quiet: a reunion, the same room, the night narrowing to two people, facts stated, a short exchange as the climax.
The midpoint invalidates what the team thought it was solving, so the rookie starts producing theories of his own.
The first story declares the form, the second reverses the investigation, and the climax withholds the device the audience expects.

terms.def: A scene-by-scene list of the story in plain sentences, one line per scene, written before any dialogue. It shows whether the order of scenes works.
terms.tanglish: Dialogue ezhudhurathukku munnaadi, oru scene-ku oru vari-nu kadhaiya varisaiyaa ezhudhuradhu. Order work aagudha-nu theriyum.

examples.note: One line per scene, for example "he is recognised and the clock starts". Each line should name what changes.
"The two are in the same room and the question changes." Quiet films need the change named most clearly.
"The case stops being what the team thought; he starts producing theories." One line per turn keeps an investigation readable.
"The second story lands and the search turns on the cop's own record." The outline shows the structure before dialogue exists.

terms.def: A short prose summary of the whole story from beginning to end, including the ending. Producers and festivals read it, and it proves the story is decided.
terms.tanglish: Kadhai muzhusaiyum, mudivu sethu, sinnadhaa ezhudhuradhu. Padikkaravanga kadhai mudivaachu-nu nambanum.

examples.note: A forged degree, a recognition, a term to clear the papers, and a choice at the end of the lie. The synopsis ends on the choice, not on a twist.
Brief on plot and honest about it: a reunion, one night, a quiet exchange, and lives that resume.
A rookie, a veteran and a methodical killer. The synopsis should say the case closes as a result of his arc completing.
An encounter cop, a gangster who tells stories, and a final question the cop has to answer for himself.

terms.def: The film written as pages: scene headings, action, character names and dialogue in a fixed format the whole crew can read. One page is roughly one minute of screen time.
terms.tanglish: Padam-a page-aa ezhudhuradhu: scene heading, action, dialogue, oru standard format-la. Oru page, oru nimidam.

examples.note: Both its comic opening and its later arithmetic have to be shown on the page: what the camera sees and what is said.
Mostly dialogue and staging: distance, who looks away first, shown through action lines.
Procedure on the page: the veteran states the rules aloud, so action and dialogue both carry the lesson.
Stories told in dialogue become scenes of their own, and the page has to give the telling to the person who profits from it.

terms.def: Everything the audience sees and hears that is not dialogue, written in the present tense. Describe only what a camera or microphone can capture.
terms.tanglish: Dialogue illaadha ellam: kaamera-la theriyaradhu, ketkuradhu. Ippo nadakkura maadhiri present tense-la ezhudhunga.

examples.note: A character performing a fluency he does not have is written as what we see him do, not as what he feels.
Distance, glances and who looks away first are action lines: the staging carries what the dialogue avoids.
The rookie's physical reaction to the work is an action line: visible, unglamorous, and never explained.
A look across a table between the cop and the gangster is action. The page shows it and does not explain it.

terms.def: The character's name in capitals above their dialogue, so the reader and the actor know who is speaking. Spell it the same way every time.
terms.tanglish: Dialogue-ku mela capital-la character peyar. Yaaru pesaraanga-nu theriya. Ovvoru thadavaiyum ore maadhiri ezhudhunga.

examples.note: RAGAVAN above his lines. The cast list and breakdown match speakers by that exact name.
RAM and JANAKI, spelled the same every time, so the cast list counts two people and not four.
PRAKASH and LOGANATHAN: the cue is the name the cast list will use, so keep it identical page to page.
VIKRAM and VEDHA: two cues in an argument. Consistent names keep the screen-time count right.

terms.def: What characters say out loud. Good dialogue sounds like speech, carries what the character wants, and often leaves the real feeling unsaid.
terms.tanglish: Character-gal pesaradhu. Nijam pesara maadhiri irukkanum, aasaiya kaatanum, unmaiyaana feeling-a sollaama vidanum.

examples.note: Early dialogue is bluff and charm: the persuasion that later indicts the protagonist.
The dialogue stays on logistics and old classmates while the staging carries the real content.
The veteran states the rules of the work aloud, so dialogue doubles as exposition and as an examination of the rookie.
Told as stories: each is a deliberate choice by the speaker, which makes dialogue an act of aggression.

terms.def: A short direction in brackets under a character name, such as (quietly) or (to the door). Use it only when the line could be read two ways.
terms.tanglish: Character peyar-ku keezha bracket-la sinna direction: (mella) maadhiri. Line-ku rendu artham varumbodhu mattum use pannunga.

examples.note: A confident pitch could be sincere or a bluff. A parenthetical settles it only where the scene does not already.
Where a plain line hides feeling, resist (sadly): let staging carry it and keep brackets for real ambiguity.
Under pressure the rookie's line might need (steadily) against a shaking read: one word of direction, not a paragraph.
When the gangster answers a question with a question, a parenthetical is rarely needed. The structure tells the actor.

terms.def: An instruction between scenes such as CUT TO: or FADE OUT. Modern scripts use few, because a clean scene heading already implies a cut.
terms.tanglish: Rendu scene-ku naduvula CUT TO: maadhiri line. Ippo romba use panna maattaanga, scene heading-e cut-nu artham.

examples.note: Most cuts between its scenes need no marking. A deliberate echo from an early joke to a later number might.
A slow evening moves from scene to scene on plain headings. A transition would add nothing.
The investigation moves by headings. Keep a marked transition for a real jump, such as a gap in time.
A cut from one story back to the interrogation is a real change, one of the few places a marked transition could earn its line.

terms.def: CONT'D beside a character name means the same person is speaking again after an action line. It tells the reader it is one speech, not a new one.
terms.tanglish: Oru character pesi, naduvula action vandhu, thirumbi avane pesinaa CONT'D. Adhu oru speech-ae.

examples.note: Ragavan's pitch is broken by a glance across the room, then resumes: his cue gets (CONT'D).
An action line sits between two lines from one person in a quiet exchange: (CONT'D) shows it is one thought.
Loganathan lists a rule, an action line breaks in, and he continues: his cue gets (CONT'D).
Vedha begins a story, a beat of action interrupts, and the telling resumes under VEDHA (CONT'D).

terms.def: Reading the script scene by scene and listing everything each scene needs: cast, props, locations, vehicles, costumes. It is the first step in planning a shoot.
terms.tanglish: Script-a scene scene-aa padichu enna enna thevai-nu list pannuradhu: cast, props, location. Shoot plan-oda modhal step.

examples.note: A breakdown separates the scenes needing a campus from the ones needing an office, and lists who is needed in each.
A story built on one evening likely has a short list of places, so the weight of its breakdown sits on cast and props.
A procedural lists recurring roles and evidence props scene by scene, which makes the working set visible.
Interrogation scenes repeat a setting, and the breakdown groups them so the shoot can combine them.

terms.def: A schedule board with one strip per scene, ordered into shoot days by location, cast and time of day. It plans the shoot, not the story order.
terms.tanglish: Oru scene-ku oru strip. Location, cast, neram paathu shoot naal-kku varisai pannuvaanga. Kadhai order illa, shoot order.

examples.note: Scenes in the same place can be grouped into one day, even when the story visits them at different times.
Scenes in one place can be shot together, in whatever order suits the cast and the light.
Scenes with both the veteran and the rookie share cast, so a stripboard can cluster them into the days both are booked.
Scenes with both leads in the same room can be clustered into the days both actors are available.

terms.def: A chart showing which days each cast member or element is needed on the shoot. It shows who is booked when and where days can be saved.
terms.tanglish: Evvalavu naal yaar-yaar thevai-nu chart. Yaar eppo booking, enga naal micham pannalam-nu theriyum.

examples.note: The protagonist works almost every day, while the dean likely needs only a few. The chart makes that visible.
Two leads carry the film, so two rows are busiest and everyone else has short blocks.
The two leads are needed on most days, and the supporting roles show as short blocks.
Three principal roles overlap in different ways, and the chart shows how that sets the booking.

terms.def: The one-page plan for a single shoot day: scenes, cast and crew call times, location, weather and notes. The assistant director issues it the day before.
terms.tanglish: Oru shoot naal-ku oru page: scene, yaaru eppo varanum, location, notes. AD munnaadi naal anuppuvaar.

examples.note: A day set in the college lists the dean's call and the lead's together, since the scene needs both of them.
A night scene lists a late call, because call times follow when the scene and the light need people.
A procedural day lists both leads' calls and the props the scene needs, so nobody waits.
An interrogation day lists both leads and the location, with times set by when the room is free.

terms.def: A list of every camera set-up for each scene: the framing, the lens, the movement. The director and cinematographer write it from the script.
terms.tanglish: Ovvoru scene-ku camera set-up list: framing, lens, movement. Director-um cinematographer-um script-la irundhu seiyyuvaanga.

examples.note: A gag meant to become arithmetic later needs a clear close shot the first time, so the audience memorises it for fun.
Where staging carries the feeling, the list needs the wide that shows the distance and the close that shows who looks away.
The rookie's physical reaction needs a close shot before the film moves on.
A face-to-face argument is planned as shot and reverse shot, and the list says which speaker each set-up favours.

terms.def: The situation the story starts from, stated as 'what if': a character, a circumstance and the pressure that makes it a story rather than a situation.
terms.tanglish: Kadhai edhula aarambikkudhu-nu 'what if' kelvi. Yaaru, entha nilaimai, edhu pressure.

examples.note: What if a man who forged his way into a career is recognised by the one person who can prove it? The 'what if' already contains the pressure.
What if two people get exactly one evening, twenty-two years late? The constraint of a single night is what turns a situation into a story.
What if the trainee is the least steady person in a room that demands steadiness? The premise puts the weakness and the job in the same frame.
What if the hunted man arranges his own capture and then only answers in stories? The inversion is the premise.

terms.def: A way of dividing a story into setup, confrontation and resolution, with a turning point at each boundary. It is a map of where pressure changes, not a formula to fill in.
terms.tanglish: Kadhaiya moonu paagam: aarambam, mothal, mudivu. Rendu idathula thirupam. Idhu map, formula illa.

examples.note: Act one is the comic con, the recognition ends it, act two is the repayment, and the choice to take the loss opens the last act.
A quiet film still has the shape: the reunion arranged, the night they are finally alone together, and a short plain exchange that does the work of a climax.
The posting and the partner open the film, the narrowing method locks act two in place, and the lone deduction belongs to act three.
The declared three stories give the film an unusually visible skeleton: each telling is a stage, and the last decision is the resolution.

terms.def: The moment a story's direction changes so completely that the audience feels a new part begin. Characters commit to something they cannot take back.
terms.tanglish: Kadhai thirumbura idam. Hero thirumba mudiyaadha mudivu edukkura nimisham.

examples.note: He accepts the dean's terms and re-enters the life he ran from. It is a humiliating decision, not a heroic one, and that is why it works as a break.
When the two are finally in the same room, the film stops being about arranging the meeting and becomes about whether either will speak plainly.
The search narrows from a general hunt to one specific method. After that the team is committed to patience, which is the thing the protagonist lacks.
The first story is told and the film's rules are declared: this will be settled by argument, not pursuit. The cop commits to listening.

terms.def: A moment inside a scene or sequence where what a character wants, knows or risks changes direction. Without one, a scene only continues.
terms.tanglish: Scene-kulla edhachum thirumbanum. Thirumbaama irundha adhu scene illa, sumaa nadakkudhu.

examples.note: The moment he stops hiding from the dean and begins counting what he owes turns the film from dodging to doing.
The conversation shifts from the group to the two of them, and the talk stops being about the past in general and starts being about this pair.
The investigation stops being about the shape the team believed and the protagonist begins to generate theories himself.
When the second story lands, the cop starts auditing his own record instead of his target's. The direction of the search reverses without a change of location.

terms.def: An image, sound, object or phrase that returns through the film and gathers meaning each time. A motif is how a theme gets said without being spoken.
terms.tanglish: Padam muzhukka thirumba thirumba varra image / sound / porul. Theme-a pesaama solla vazhi.

examples.note: The running number joke returns as a workload with a deadline. Same object, changed meaning, and the repetition is what carries the theme.
Kept objects and the music that marks memory return across the night. Each reappearance means a little more than the last.
Sound recurs as information the dialogue refuses to state. By the end the audience listens the way the investigators do.
The story-within-a-story form is itself a motif: each telling repeats the shape, so a change in the shape is felt immediately.

terms.def: An object or goal that everyone in the story chases, which matters because of what the chase does to the people, not for what it is.
terms.tanglish: Ellarum thedura oru porul. Adhu enna-nu mukkiyam illa, thedurathula aal enna aaraanga-nu thaan mukkiyam.

examples.note: The degree is the chase object. What it is barely matters; what matters is what keeping it costs the people around him.
There is hardly a chase object at all; the nearest is the evening itself, which shows a story can run on a human wish with nothing to carry.
The case is the nominal object. The real story is whether the trainee can hold his nerve, and the case only gives that test a reason to happen.
Whoever is caught, and for whatever, is a pretext. The film is about what the stories do to the one who listens.

terms.def: Hints early in a story that prepare the audience for what comes later. Done well, it is only visible on the second viewing.
terms.tanglish: Pinnaadi varadhu pathi munnaadiye chinna hint. Rendaavadhu paakumbodhu thaan theriyum.

examples.note: The number used as a joke early is quietly a preview of the load he must clear later. The comic setup is also a warning.
The film shows how ordinary his life is before the reunion, which foreshadows what the reunion will interrupt.
A habit of the trainee, shown as a quirk, hints at the quality that will eventually decide the case.
The film announces its own folk-tale structure at the start, which foreshadows the pattern its final choice will break.

terms.def: When the audience knows something a character does not, so every scene is read with a second layer of tension.
terms.tanglish: Audience-kku theriyum, character-kku theriyaadhu. Adhaala ovvoru dialogue-um rendu artham.

examples.note: While the protagonist performs a fluency he lacks, the audience already holds the secret, and every confident line becomes funny and dangerous at once.
The audience feels how much each of them leaves unsaid, even where the two pretend the evening is only logistics.
When the trainee misses a detail the audience has noticed, the scene is read as tension because the viewer is ahead of him.
Because the film tells us the form up front, we know a story is coming that will cost the listener, and we watch him walk into it.

terms.def: A fact, object or line placed early so that a later event feels earned instead of convenient. The cousin of a setup, seen from the writer's side.
terms.tanglish: Munnaadiye vechu vidura vishayam. Appuram vandhaa 'convenient'-a illa, 'earned'-a theriyum.

examples.note: The comic number is planted as a joke, so its later return as a deadline needs no explanation.
A kept object is planted as evidence of years, so the audience trusts what it says about the characters without a line of dialogue.
The decisive observation is hidden inside characterisation so it slips past the audience's relevance filter and returns as the solution.
Each story plants something the next picks up, so the final question can only be answered with what the film has already placed.

terms.def: A clue that looks important and points the wrong way. It keeps the audience guessing without cheating, as long as it can be explained afterwards.
terms.tanglish: Thappa vazhi kaattura clue. Padam mudinjadhum 'adhu ippadi dhaan'-nu explain panna mudiyanum.

examples.note: A character who looks like danger turns out to be principle. The audience braces for a villain and meets a rule.
The film tempts us towards the usual romance reversal and then declines it, so the genre's promise works as a red herring.
Early theories about the killer's method fall apart at the midpoint, and the film lets the team, and the audience, chase the wrong pattern.
The audience is invited to take sides between cop and gangster, and the film uses that expectation as the thing it later withdraws.

terms.def: A secondary storyline running alongside the main one, usually a relationship, that lets the theme be seen from a second side.
terms.tanglish: Main kadhaiyoda koodave oru chinna kadhai. Theme-a vera kodhalil kaattum.

examples.note: The classmate who pays for the shortcut is the film's second line. Through that story the cost of the con is shown in human terms.
With almost no plot, the second line is the lives each will carry back at the end, which is the pressure beneath the single night.
The partner relationship, senior against junior, is a story of its own and is where the theme of nerve is actually argued.
A character who holds the principle the cop claims to hold lives inside his own house, and her line is the second argument on the same theme.

terms.def: The closing movement after the climax: the new normal. It shows what the climax changed and lets the audience leave the world.
terms.tanglish: Climax-ku appuram: ippo vazhkai eppadi maariduchu-nu kaattura paagam.

examples.note: The life that remains is smaller than the invented one and better founded. The ending presents the reduction as enough, not as punishment.
The lives resume. The film declines to reward the audience with a reversal, and the refusal is the ending's argument.
The closing movement treats the work as continuing, with the protagonist changed but marked.
The ending declines to arbitrate. Both positions stay arguable and the film closes on the protagonist's choice, not on a verdict.

terms.def: A big, planned scene built to be remembered: a chase, a confrontation, a performance. It still has to move the story, not pause it.
terms.tanglish: Padathulayae oru perusa, plan panni vecha scene. Kadhaiyum munnaadi poganum.

examples.note: The recognition scene is the film's biggest turn, and it is a conversation, not a stunt. A set piece can be a room and a decision.
The reunion night is the set piece: one occasion, held to carry the whole film.
The lone deduction at the climax is staged as the film's set piece, with the arc completing first and the case closing as a consequence.
Each telling of a story is a small set piece built on the same shape, so the difference between them can be felt.

terms.def: A run of scenes that together do one job in the story, with a beginning, a middle and a result. A film is a chain of them.
terms.tanglish: Onnu rendu scene illa, oru velaya seyyura scene-gal thodar. Padam = sequence-gal.

examples.note: The stretch where he starts clearing his papers is one sequence: a goal, setbacks and a result that shifts his position with the dean.
The long evening, from the group to the two of them alone, is a sequence even though nothing external happens.
The narrowing of the search, from the general hunt to the specific method, is one sequence with a clear start and result.
Each of the three tellings is a sequence with a set structure, which is why a change in the structure is noticed at once.

terms.def: A scene set earlier than the main story, used to show something the present needs. It earns its place only if it changes how we read the present.
terms.tanglish: Pazhaya kaalathu scene. Ippo nadakkura vishayatha purinjukka udhavanum.

examples.note: The forged past is the film's engine; showing it once would give the present its weight, but the comedy works because the audience gets the facts without it.
Memory is the film's subject, so time past arrives where the present cannot say it, cued by music rather than explained.
A flash to an earlier case would only earn its place if it changed how the audience reads the trainee's present fear.
Each story the gangster tells plays like a flashback, shaped by the teller to push the listener towards an answer.

terms.def: A prose telling of the whole film, scene by scene, in the present tense and without dialogue. It lets you test the story before the expensive work of formatting a script.
terms.tanglish: Padathoda muzhu kadhaiya present tense-la, dialogue illama, prose-a ezhudhuradhu. Script ezhudhumunnaadi kadhai odudha-nu paakka.

examples.note: A treatment would let you check that the comic setup and the later reckoning really line up before a single scene is formatted.
A treatment of the reunion night would quickly show whether an evening with almost no plot still builds, scene by scene.
In prose the investigation's order of discovery can be audited: does each step narrow the case, and when does the trainee finally act alone?
A treatment makes the three-story architecture checkable on one page: what each telling costs the cop, and whether the last question is answered by him.

terms.def: A unit of story set in one place and time, in which someone wants something and something changes. If nothing changes, cut it or combine it.
terms.tanglish: Oru idam, oru neram, oru velai. Edhavadhu maaranum, illa-na cut pannidunga.

examples.note: A scene between the protagonist and the dean is one place and one goal: the first changes what each can demand of the other.
Even the quietest scene changes something: who looks away first, who says what they came to say, who leaves it unsaid.
A scene of procedure is a character test as well, so the briefing changes the relationship between trainee and veteran.
A scene of one story being told is a contest: by its end the listener has been moved to a position he did not hold before.

terms.def: Voice-over: a voice heard on the soundtrack but not from a person on screen in the scene, such as narration or a remembered line. Written as (V.O.) beside the character's name.
terms.tanglish: Screen-la aal illa, aana kural ketkum: narration, ninaivu. Cue pakkathula (V.O.)-nu ezhudhuvom.

examples.note: A confident narration over the con in act one would sell the lie to the audience, and then its later silence would cost the character.
A remembered line over an image of the past is a way to carry memory without leaving the present scene.
A report read in voice-over could bridge a gap in the investigation, but it hands the audience the facts, so it should be used sparingly.
A teller's voice over the image of his story is the film's natural device, since the narration is itself a move in the contest.

terms.def: Off-screen: the speaker is in the scene but out of frame. Written (O.S.) beside the name. It keeps a character present without showing them.
terms.tanglish: Character scene-la irukkaanga, aana frame-ku veliya. Cue pakkathula (O.S.).

examples.note: The dean's voice from beyond the frame keeps his pressure present in a scene even when the camera stays on the protagonist.
A voice calling across a room can place the second person in the scene, and the camera can stay with the one who will not look.
A veteran's instruction heard off-screen lets the camera hold the trainee's face while the partner's authority is still in the scene.
An off-screen line from the gangster can keep him in the room while the camera is on the cop's reaction.

terms.def: Printed at the bottom of a page when a character's speech runs on to the next page, with (CONT'D) after the name on the new page. Software adds it; you do not type it.
terms.tanglish: Oru speech adutha page-ku poidhuna, kizhe (MORE), adutha page-la (CONT'D). Software thaanaave podum.

examples.note: A long argument by the dean that spans a page break carries (MORE) and then (CONT'D), so the actor and the reader know it is one speech.
A long speech in a dialogue-led, quiet film stands out on the page because it needs a (MORE).
A veteran's long explanation of procedure may split across pages, and (MORE) tells the reader he is not done.
A long story told by the gangster routinely breaks across pages and is marked (MORE) and (CONT'D).

terms.def: A run of short shots, often with music, that compresses time or shows a change without scenes in between. Write it as a list of images that adds up to one idea.
terms.tanglish: Neraiya chinna shot, music-oda, neram-a surukki kaattum. Oru list-a ezhudhi, mothama oru artham varanum.

examples.note: His rushed attempt to clear his papers is an obvious montage: a pile of work shown through brief images of effort and the shrinking calendar.
A film this still has little need for montage, which makes the occasional run of images stand out as memory rather than action.
The slow narrowing of the case can be written as a montage of repeated checking, to show time passing without a scene for each step.
A montage would work against the form here, since each telling is a full scene and the film depends on its not being compressed.

terms.def: Switching back and forth between two places or two actions that are happening at the same time, so each comments on the other. Written INTERCUT in the script.
terms.tanglish: Rendu idathula nadakkuradha maari maari kaatturadhu. Onnu innoru onnukku artham kodukkum.

examples.note: Cutting between his exam hall and the person who is paying for his mistake lets the comedy of one place bear the cost of the other.
Cutting between the two of them in separate places lets the film put their silences next to each other.
Cutting between the trainee alone and the veteran far away lets the audience see how much he is relying on someone who is not there.
Cutting between the telling and what the listener is doing with it puts the cost of a story in the same moment as the story.

terms.def: A scene before the title that starts the story straight away, with no introduction. It establishes tone and a question the audience wants answered.
terms.tanglish: Title-ku munnaadiye kadhai aarambam. Tone-um oru kelviyum kudukkum.

examples.note: An opening in a comic register shows him performing a fluency he does not have, which establishes tone and a question before anything else.
An opening on the protagonist alone at work sets the baseline the rest of the film will be measured against.
An opening that shows the investigation's machinery as routine sets the standard against which the trainee's unsteadiness will read.
An opening that announces the folk-tale form states the rules of the game up front.

terms.def: A set of drawings, one per planned shot, showing framing and action before the shoot. It does not need to be good art; it needs to be clear.
terms.tanglish: Ovvoru shot-kum oru chinna drawing. Artist-a irukkanum-nu avasiyam illa, purinjaa podhum.

examples.note: A frame for the comic setup, a frame for the same object when it returns as a deadline: the board shows the audience's memory being used.
Two frames, a wide that shows the distance between them and a close that shows who looks away, can carry the whole logic of the reunion's first recognition.
A frame of the trainee in the corner of a room and the veteran in the foreground says more about their relationship than a line of dialogue.
Panels of a listener's face in each telling show that the camera should stay with him while the voice does the work.

terms.def: A short collection of images, colours and references that fixes the film's look and tone, shared with the cinematographer, designer and costume team before the shoot.
terms.tanglish: Padathoda look-ku reference images thokuppu. Camera, art, costume ellarum ore kodhal-la irukka.

examples.note: A lookbook would pair the corporate polish of his fake life with the worn corridors of the college, so the cost of the con is visible in the look.
References for a school reunion and a long evening would fix a soft, lived-in look in which restraint reads as warmth, not coldness.
References for a patient, procedural thriller would fix a cold and controlled look in which waiting is the dominant image.
References for a folk-tale told in a city of noir would fix a look in which the stories can feel different from the frame story.

terms.def: A visit to a possible location to check light, sound, space, power, access and permission before committing to it. Recce comes from 'reconnaissance'.
terms.tanglish: Shoot pannum idatha munnaadiye poi paakurathu: velicham, sound, space, current, permission.

examples.note: A college corridor needs a recce for quiet at the hour you want to shoot and for whether the dean's office can hold a camera and two actors.
A reunion night needs a venue that can be dark enough for the evening and quiet enough to record a plain conversation.
An interrogation or investigation room needs checking for space to move a camera and for outside noise that would intrude on the quiet the film depends on.
A room for a long two-person contest needs a recce for room tone and for how many angles it can really give.

terms.def: Choosing the actors for each role, through auditions, screen tests and conversation. Good casting is half of direction.
terms.tanglish: Yaaru entha role-nu theduradhu: audition, screen test. Nalla casting-eh paadhi direction.

examples.note: A comic con-man who can turn into a man paying a real price needs an actor who can play both without a join, and a dean who can be correct without being cruel.
The film asks two leads to hold a long night mostly through restraint, so casting is about whether they can say the unsaid with their faces.
The trainee must read as unsteady and the veteran as the standard of composure, so the pairing has to be tested together.
The cop and the gangster must be matched in presence for a contest of stories to feel even, so the pair is cast as a pair.

terms.def: The plan of which scenes are shot on which days. It groups by location, cast availability and light, not by story order.
terms.tanglish: Entha naal entha scene-nu plan. Kadhai order illa, location / cast / velicham paathu group pannuvom.

examples.note: College scenes can be grouped together even if they fall at the start and the end of the story.
The reunion venue is shot as one block, even though the evening moves through the film in order.
Scenes that share one location, such as the investigation room, are shot together across story time.
The scenes of a single room can be grouped, but the cop's changing state across them needs to be tracked for continuity.

terms.def: The person who runs the set and the schedule so the director can direct. The AD keeps the day on time and issues the call sheet.
terms.tanglish: Director direct panna, set-um schedule-um AD paakkuvaar. Call sheet-um avar thaan.

examples.note: A comic day full of crowds and a quiet drama day need very different handling; the AD plans the order so the cast and extras are used well.
A night shoot with two leads needs the AD to protect the time and quiet the scene depends on.
A day of repeated procedural scenes needs an AD to keep the order straight and the rooms free.
A day with two leads and long takes needs an AD to protect the actors' time and the room's.

terms.def: Everything the camera sees that was designed: sets, locations dressed, colour, props and the overall visual world. It tells the audience who lives here.
terms.tanglish: Camera-la theriyura ellaam design: set, color, props. 'Idhu yaaroda idam'-nu solla vendiya.

examples.note: A fake life in a corporate setting against the worn college of his past is told by dressing alone: polish on one side and wear on the other.
Kept things, worn things: what has been preserved and what has been replaced does the work of exposition about two decades.
The investigative rooms are set up as routine and competent first so the trainee's unsteadiness reads against them.
The settings of each telling can be given their own look so that the audience feels the move between stories without being told.

terms.def: Written permission from the owner or authority to film at a place. Without it, a shoot can be stopped at its worst moment.
terms.tanglish: Antha idathula shoot panna ezhuthu-la anumathi. Illa-na nadunthula niruthiduvaanga.

examples.note: A college or office location needs permission from its authority, and the person who recognises him on camera is not the one you want to ask on the day.
A public place or venue for an evening needs permission for the hours and crowd it will bring.
A police or institutional setting would need clear permission and rules about what may be shown.
A public street or building used for a chase or a capture needs permission and often a plan for crowds.

terms.def: Money and time set aside for the things that will go wrong: weather, illness, a lost day. Producers add a percentage to the budget for it.
terms.tanglish: Thappaa poga vaaippulla vishayatukku munnaadiye vecha panam / neram. Budget-la oru percent.

examples.note: A film with crowds and outdoor days needs a margin for the day it rains, not just a plan for when it does not.
A night shoot across one venue has little room to recover a lost evening, so a reserve of time is the safeguard.
A procedural built on long, tense scenes cannot be rushed, so time reserved for a bad day protects the performances.
A film built on two-hander scenes depends on both actors being present, so a day lost to illness needs a plan.

terms.def: An indoor or alternative location lined up in advance so the crew can still shoot something useful if weather or access ruins the planned scene.
terms.tanglish: Mazhai-na plan A poidum. Indoor-la shoot panna plan B location. Adhuthaan cover set.

examples.note: If rain stops a campus exterior, a corridor or classroom scene gives the day something useful to shoot.
If a night exterior is lost, an interior scene from the same evening can be shot in its place.
If an outdoor scene is rained off, an interior investigative scene can fill the day.
If an exterior chase cannot be shot, a one-room telling can replace it, since its needs are small.

terms.def: Working through scenes with the actors before the camera rolls, to find the blocking, the rhythm and the problems while they are cheap to fix.
terms.tanglish: Camera odaradhukku munnaadi actor-oda scene-a pannipaakkuradhu. Prechana mudhale theriyum.

examples.note: A scene where he must lie fluently and the dean must stay calm is worth rehearsing so that the comedy lands and the threat stays real.
A film that lives on what is not said needs rehearsal to find where the pauses and looks go.
Rehearsal lets the veteran's cold instruction and the trainee's hesitation find a rhythm that reads as truth.
The contest of questions between the two leads rewards rehearsal, since the timing of each reply is the scene.

terms.def: Deciding where the actors stand and move within a scene, and where the camera is in relation to them. It tells the story with positions.
terms.tanglish: Actor enga nikkaraanga, eppadi nagarraanga, camera enga-nu mudivu. Position-aaley kadhai solrom.

examples.note: Putting the dean seated and the protagonist standing in the same room says who holds the power before a word is spoken.
Distance across a room and who is the first to look away is the entire content of the scene, so the blocking is the writing.
The veteran at the front of the frame and the trainee behind him can show reliance on a partner without a line of dialogue.
Who sits and who stands across the table, and who rises first, tells the audience where the contest stands.

terms.def: The time a person must arrive on set. It differs by role: makeup and camera often come before the actors, who are called when the scene needs them.
terms.tanglish: Set-ku varanum-nu sollura neram. Ovvoru role-kum vera neram.

examples.note: A scene with the dean and the lead calls both of them together, while an extra for a crowd shot may be called hours later.
A night scene means a late call for everyone, with the lights and camera set before the actors arrive.
A day of two-hander scenes calls both leads at the same time, and the crew a good while before.
A day in one room calls the leads when the room is ready, and the crew earlier to build the light.

terms.def: The board shown at the start of a take, with scene, shot and take numbers, and the clap that lets sound and picture be matched later. Called out as 'scene 12, shot 3, take 2'.
terms.tanglish: Take aarambathula board: scene, shot, take number. Clap sound-um picture-um match panna.

examples.note: A day of comic set-ups with many repeats needs a clear slate so the editor can find the take where the timing worked.
A scene played with one or two long takes still needs the slate, because the edit will choose between them on performance alone.
A procedural with many angles on the same room needs exact slates to keep the shots straight in the edit.
Long, back-to-back takes of a two-person scene are easily mixed up in the edit unless the slate is clear.

terms.def: One recording of a shot, from 'action' to 'cut'. A shot usually takes several until the director has the performance and the camera has the move.
terms.tanglish: Oru shot-ku 'action'-la irundhu 'cut' varaikkum oru take. Sariyaa varra varaikkum thirumba edukkuvom.

examples.note: A joke needs several takes to find the exact pause that makes it funny, and the film's later seriousness depends on that timing.
A scene of restraint may need many takes to find the one in which the silence is neither too much nor too little.
A scene of the trainee's reaction needs enough takes that the director can choose the one that reads as fear, not acting.
A scene of a story told across a table may need many takes to find the rhythm of question and answer.

terms.def: Keeping everything that should match from shot to shot actually matching: costume, props, hair, position, what is in the glass. Breaks are noticed in the edit.
terms.tanglish: Shot-ku shot ottanum: dress, prop, hair, position. Maari irundha edit-la theriyum.

examples.note: A scene shot over two days must keep the dean's papers and the protagonist's tie the same so the cut feels like one conversation.
A long evening shot out of order must keep drinks, light and hair consistent so it reads as one night.
A case built from clues needs exact continuity of the objects the audience is asked to remember.
A long argument shot across angles needs the cop's state and the objects on the table to match from cut to cut.

terms.def: The crew member who watches every take against the script, noting continuity, what was shot, what was said and which takes the director liked.
terms.tanglish: Script paathukittu ovvoru take-la enna nadandhadhu note panni, continuity paakkura aal.

examples.note: A scene with a running number joke needs the supervisor to make sure the wording and counts match between shots.
A long evening with small gestures needs the supervisor to log every drink and glance so that cuts are clean.
A procedural built on clues needs a supervisor to confirm that the audience is shown exactly what the script says.
A scene of repeated questions and answers needs the supervisor to track which lines were covered in each angle.

terms.def: Digital imaging technician: the person who checks the camera's picture, copies and backs up the footage safely and prepares it for the edit. A lost card is a lost day.
terms.tanglish: Camera-la irundhu footage-a safe-a copy panni, backup vechu, picture-a check pannuravar.

examples.note: On a long college shoot with many cards a day, the DIT keeps every copy verified so none of the day's takes are lost.
A night shoot means every card matters; the DIT checks the dark images are exposed properly and saved twice.
A procedural shot in dark rooms needs the DIT to check the picture and the backups before the crew moves on.
A film built on long performances cannot afford a lost card, so the DIT copies and checks twice.

terms.def: The end of shooting for a scene, a day or the whole film. 'That's a wrap' means the crew is done. After wrap the gear is returned and the paperwork closed.
terms.tanglish: Shoot mudinjadhu: scene, naal, illa mothama padam. Appuram gear thirumba kudukkanum.

examples.note: At the end of a day in the college, wrap means the dean's scene is done and the location can be released.
At the end of the night, wrap means the venue is returned as it was found.
At the end of a day of procedural scenes, wrap means the rooms are cleared and the footage backed up.
At the end of a day in one room, wrap means the set can be struck and the day's cards verified.

terms.def: Shooting a scene from enough angles and distances that the editor has choices. The standard set is master, close-ups of each speaker, and inserts.
terms.tanglish: Oru scene-a pala angle, pala distance-la edukkuradhu. Editor-kku choice irukkum.

examples.note: A conversation between the lead and the dean is covered wide for power, then in close-ups for each reaction, so the cut can choose whose face carries the line.
Where a scene lives on distance and who looks away, coverage needs the wide that shows the gap and the close that shows the glance.
A scene of the trainee reacting needs a close of his face as well as the shot of what he sees, so the cut can hold on fear.
A scene of question and answer is covered as shot and reverse shot, with enough extra to vary the rhythm.

terms.def: One wide shot that plays the whole scene from start to end, so the editor always has something to fall back on. The other angles are then shot to match it.
terms.tanglish: Mothama scene-a wide-la oru thadavai oda vitta shot. Matha angle ellam adhoda match aagum.

examples.note: A conversation with the dean played in one wide shows the whole space and the distance between the two before the film moves in.
A master of the reunion's first meeting holds the group and the two of them in one frame, showing how the distance between them is the content.
A master of the investigation room shows how the team works as a machine before the film narrows to the trainee.
A master of the two leads across a table holds the whole contest at once and lets the audience judge who is winning.

terms.def: A wide shot, often an exterior, that tells the audience where and when a scene is. It lets the following scene skip the explaining.
terms.tanglish: Idhu enga, eppo-nu kaattura wide shot. Adhukku appuram scene-la explain pannanum-nu avasiyam illa.

examples.note: A shot of the college gate places the audience in the past he ran from, so the next scene needs no explaining.
A shot of the venue at night tells us where the evening happens and what time it is.
A shot of the station or building the team works from tells us what kind of world this is before a single line is spoken.
A shot of the city or the interrogation building places each telling and marks the shift between them.

terms.def: A shot framing a face or a detail so closely that it fills the screen. It tells the audience what a character feels, or what to look at.
terms.tanglish: Mugam illa oru porul-a screen muzhuka kaattura shot. Character enna feel pannraanga-nu theriyum.

examples.note: A close on his face when the dean recognises him tells the audience the whole con is about to end without a word.
A close on a face that does not say what it feels holds the scene's tension in a silence.
A close on the trainee's face during the first hard moment tells the audience what the work costs him.
A close on the listener's face as the story ends shows what the telling has done to him.

terms.def: A close shot of an object or detail, such as a letter, a phone screen or a key, cut into a scene to give information or emphasis.
terms.tanglish: Kaiyila irukkura letter, phone, key maadhiri oru porul-oda close shot. Thagaval kudukka.

examples.note: An insert of a page with a count on it gives the audience the number before the dialogue names it, and later returns as a deadline.
An insert of a kept object tells us what has been held on to without a line of explanation.
An insert of the small detail that turns out to matter has to be planted so ordinarily that it is easy to miss.
An insert of a notebook or a file lets the audience read what the cop would rather not say aloud.

terms.def: A shot of something other than the main action, cut in briefly: a reaction, a clock, a crowd. It hides a join or adds a second meaning.
terms.tanglish: Main action-ku vera ondrukku oru short cut. Reaction, clock, crowd. Join-a maraikkum, artham sollum.

examples.note: A cutaway to a classmate's face during the dean's reckoning shows the cost to the person who did not take the shortcut.
A cutaway to a small object or someone watching from across a room can carry what the dialogue refuses to say.
A cutaway to a colleague during the trainee's hesitation lets the audience see what the room thinks of him.
A cutaway to a witness while the story is being told shows the audience how it is landing.

terms.def: A shot from a character's position, showing what they see. It places the audience inside their head, so use it where their view matters.
terms.tanglish: Oru character paakkura maari camera. Audience avanga thalaikkulla poidum.

examples.note: A shot from his eyes of a hall of waiting students puts the audience inside the fear of being found out.
A shot from one person's eyes across the room is how the film can say what neither will say aloud.
A shot from the trainee's eyes at a scene he cannot bear to look at makes the audience look away with him.
A shot from the listener's side as the gangster speaks puts the audience in the chair the cop is in.

terms.def: A shot with two people in the frame. It shows their relationship, who is close, who is turned away, better than separate close-ups can.
terms.tanglish: Rendu per oru frame-la. Rendu perukkum ulla uravu theriyum: yaaru kitta, yaaru vilagi.

examples.note: A two-shot of the protagonist and the dean shows how far apart they are, which a cut between them would hide.
A two-shot of the pair keeps the distance between them on screen, which is the content of the scene.
A two-shot of the trainee beside the veteran shows how much he leans on someone he cannot match.
A two-shot of the cop and the gangster across a table shows them as equals in the room.

terms.def: A shot of one person seen past the shoulder of another. It keeps the listener in the frame and is the standard way to shoot a conversation.
terms.tanglish: Oruthar-oda thozhukku pinnaadi irundhu innoruthar-a paakkura shot. Pesura scene-ku standard.

examples.note: Over the dean's shoulder to the protagonist, the audience sees his bluff land on a man who knows better.
Over one shoulder to the other face, the audience sees what is said and who is listening at once.
Over the veteran's shoulder to the trainee, the audience sees the instruction and the trainee's face in one frame.
Over the gangster's shoulder to the cop, the audience sees the story land on the listener.

terms.def: Keep the camera on one side of an imaginary line between two characters, so left and right stay consistent from shot to shot. Crossing it confuses the audience.
terms.tanglish: Rendu per naduvula oru kaarpanai kodu. Camera adhu oru pakkam mattum iruntha, left-right maaraadhu.

examples.note: In a scene between lead and dean, keeping the camera on one side means he stays on the same side of the frame in every cut.
In a long conversation of two people, a stable line means we never lose track of who is where in the room.
In an interview room, keeping the line stable makes the geography of the room clear, so the audience can focus on the performance.
In a long two-hander, crossing the line on purpose is a tool: it can say that the positions have swapped.

terms.def: A camera mounted on wheels or a track so it can move smoothly toward, away from or alongside the action. A slow dolly in can say a character is being cornered.
terms.tanglish: Camera-va wheel / track-la vechu nagarththura. Nidhaanamaa munnaadi poona, character-a ottikitta maari irukkum.

examples.note: A slow move in on the protagonist as the dean says the number would turn the comic moment into a threat.
A very slow move across the room would breach the film's stillness, so a still camera is the wiser choice.
A slow move in on the trainee as the case turns would tighten the pressure without a line of dialogue.
A slow move in on the listener during a telling would show how deeply it has taken hold.

terms.def: A camera on a long arm that can rise, fall and swing across a scene. Used for a grand reveal or to pull away from a character and make them small.
terms.tanglish: Neenda arm-la camera. Mela kezha, pakka-vaa swing aagum. Perusaa kaatta illa, character-a sirusaa kaatta.

examples.note: Pulling up and away from the protagonist after his world has changed would make the character small beside the life he invented.
A rising shot at the end of the night could show the two of them as small against the city, but the film favours stillness.
A rise above the investigation room would show the team as a machine and the trainee as one part of it.
A pull-away from the room at the end of a telling would shrink both men against the world they argue about.

terms.def: A body-worn or motorised stabiliser that lets the camera move smoothly through space while the operator walks. Gives a floating, continuous feel.
terms.tanglish: Camera-va udambula maatti nadandhaalum asaiyaama irukkura stabiliser. Mithakkura maari smooth-a irukkum.

examples.note: A walk with the protagonist through the college, uncut, would put the audience inside the corridor he fled, step by step.
A film this still would use a floating camera only where memory is meant to feel loose, so the movement itself becomes a signal.
A walk behind the trainee through the building, in one move, keeps the audience with him as he decides to act.
A walk with the cop as he leaves a room could stay unbroken to show he cannot get out of the story's reach.

terms.def: How wide or narrow a lens sees, in millimetres. A wide lens takes in space and exaggerates distance; a long lens flattens it and isolates a face.
terms.tanglish: Lens evvalavu wide-a paakkum-nu mm-la. Wide: idam perusa theriyum. Long: mugam mattum, thookki kaattum.

examples.note: A wide lens in the college corridor can make the space feel large and the protagonist small, while a long lens on the dean isolates his certainty.
A longer lens across the room compresses the distance between the two and makes it feel closer than it is.
A wide lens in the investigation room exaggerates space around a trainee who does not know where to stand.
A long lens on the listener's face during a telling makes the room fall away and leaves only the story.

terms.def: How much of the picture, from near to far, is in sharp focus. Shallow depth isolates one thing; deep depth keeps the whole scene readable.
terms.tanglish: Munnaadi pinnaadi evvalavu sharp-a irukku. Shallow: oru vishayam mattum, deep: ellaamey theriyum.

examples.note: Shallow focus on the dean in a crowded hall isolates his certainty, while deep focus lets the protagonist's panic play in the background.
Shallow focus isolates a face from the room's chatter, so the unsaid is the only thing the audience can read.
Deep focus keeps both the veteran and the trainee sharp in one frame, so their relationship is visible without a cut.
Shallow focus on the listener makes the world outside his chair vanish for the length of the story.

terms.def: The shape of the frame: width compared with height. 1.85:1 is a standard wide frame; 2.39:1 is a very wide one. The choice affects composition and how the film is delivered.
terms.tanglish: Frame-oda agalam : ayaram. 1.85 normal wide, 2.39 romba wide. Composition-yum delivery-yum maarum.

examples.note: A wide frame leaves room for a hall of people around the lead, while a narrower one would press in on him.
A wider frame gives the distance between two people more room to mean something.
A wide frame gives the investigation room space and makes a lone figure in it look exposed.
A wide frame holds two men across a table and the air between them equally.

terms.def: Look-up table: a preset that maps the camera's flat, wide-range picture to a finished-looking one. Used on set to preview the look, and later as a starting point for the grade.
terms.tanglish: Camera-oda flat picture-a, mudindha look-a maathura preset. Set-la preview-ku, appuram grade-ku starting point.

examples.note: A LUT lets the crew see the warm polish of his fake life against the cooler college from the first day, not after the edit.
A LUT that holds soft, warm colour lets the crew judge whether a night scene looks lived-in on the monitor.
A LUT with cold, controlled colour lets the director check that the investigative look holds from scene to scene.
A LUT can give each of the stories its own tint on set so the cut between them is felt.

terms.def: The footage from the previous shooting day, copied and viewed by the director and key crew. Also called rushes. It is where problems are found while a reshoot is still cheap.
terms.tanglish: Mundhaiya naal edutha footage, maraanaal paakkuradhu. Prechana irundhaa reshoot panna innum easy.

examples.note: Watching the comic scenes the next morning shows whether the timing that sells the lie is really there, while the sets are still standing.
Watching the night's footage the next day shows whether the restraint reads or whether the performance has gone flat.
Watching the previous day's procedural scenes shows whether the information the audience must see actually made it into frame.
Watching the two-person scenes shows whether the rhythm of question and answer holds across the angles.

terms.def: The first joining of all the shot scenes in script order, uncut and long. Its job is to show what you have, not to look good.
terms.tanglish: Ellaa scene-um script order-la ottina mudhal pass. Neelama irukkum. Enna irukku-nu paakkura step.

examples.note: The first assembly of the film shows how much of the comic setup survives and how long the reckoning really needs.
The assembly of a film made of long scenes shows at once whether the evening holds together or drags.
The assembly of the investigation shows whether each step narrows the case, and where the film waits too long.
The assembly of three tellings shows whether the form is clear and the last decision lands.

terms.def: A first edit with structure and rhythm but unfinished: scenes trimmed, music and sound placeholder. Used to find what the film is, not to polish it.
terms.tanglish: Mudhal edit: structure irukku, aana mudiyala. Padam enna-nu kandupidikka.

examples.note: The rough cut shows whether the shift from comedy to reckoning arrives at the right moment, before any polish hides the problem.
The rough cut shows whether the single night builds or only passes, and which looks and silences can be shortened.
The rough cut shows whether the investigation's waiting is tension or drag, and whether the midpoint turn is clear.
