The rough cut shows whether the declared structure carries the audience through the three stories.

terms.def: A refined edit in which pacing, performance choices and transitions are settled and only small changes remain. The step before picture lock.
terms.tanglish: Pacing, performance ellam thaan mudivu aagiduchu; chinna maatram mattum. Picture lock-ku munnaadi.

examples.note: A fine cut of the film trims the comic setup to its sharpest so that the later payoff costs nothing to remember.
A fine cut is where the length of a look or a silence is chosen, which in this film is most of what the edit does.
A fine cut tightens the investigation so that every step moves the case and the waiting stays tense.
A fine cut balances the three tellings so that none outstays its place and the final choice lands.

terms.def: The point at which the edit is final and no more frames may be added or removed. Sound, music, colour and effects work depend on it, so changes afterwards are costly.
terms.tanglish: Edit final. Inimey frame kootta kuraikka koodaadhu. Sound, music, colour ellaam idhukku appuram thaan.

examples.note: Once locked, the dean's reckoning cannot be shortened by a few seconds without breaking every cue laid against it.
Once locked, the length of the final silence is fixed, and the music laid against it must fit.
Once locked, the placement of each clue is fixed, and sound design can be built around it.
Once locked, each telling's length is fixed, so the music and sound for each can be made to measure.

terms.def: A list of every clip in the edit with its source, in and out points and place in the timeline, so the same cut can be rebuilt in another system. Sometimes called the edit sheet.
terms.tanglish: Edit-la ovvoru clip-um enga irundhu, evvalavu, timeline-la enga-nu list. Vera software-la adhey cut-a thirumba seiyya.

examples.note: The list of every clip lets the colour and sound teams rebuild the exact cut of the comic and reckoning scenes in their own systems.
A long film built on long shots has a short list, which makes the edit easy to hand over without a mistake.
A film with many cut-ins and inserts has a long list, so an accurate EDL is what keeps the investigation rebuilt correctly.
A film with three similar tellings needs a clean list so the right takes of each are conformed to the right scenes.

terms.def: Rebuilding the locked edit from the original, highest-quality camera files rather than the small working copies used in the edit, ready for colour and finishing.
terms.tanglish: Lock aana edit-a, original camera files-la thirumba pannuradhu, colour-ku munnaadi.

examples.note: The cut is rebuilt from the original camera files so the fine grade of the corporate life against the college is done on the best picture.
The cut is rebuilt on the best files so the soft night images are graded with their full range.
The cut is rebuilt on the originals so dark rooms keep their detail through the grade.
The cut is rebuilt on the originals so the look of each telling can be set properly.

terms.def: Setting the final colour and contrast of every shot: first making shots match, then giving the film its look. The grade shapes mood as much as lighting does.
terms.tanglish: Ovvoru shot-oda colour / contrast set panradhu: mudhalla ellaam match aaganum, appuram film-oda look.

examples.note: Grade can separate the polish of his invented life from the worn colour of the college, so the film's two worlds are visible at a glance.
Grade can hold a soft, warm look across a night shot over many hours, so the evening feels like one.
Grade can hold a cold, controlled look through every investigation room, so tension is never undone by a colour mismatch.
Grade can give each telling its own tint so that the audience feels the move between stories before the dialogue says so.

terms.def: Automated dialogue replacement: re-recording an actor's lines in a studio to replace noisy or unusable on-set sound. Also called dubbing or looping.
terms.tanglish: Set-la sound sari illa-na, studio-la actor thirumba pesi record pannuradhu. Dubbing-nu solluvom.

examples.note: A crowded campus scene where the dean's voice is lost in noise can be re-recorded so every word of the reckoning is clear.
A quiet scene whose whisper was spoiled by a passing sound can be recorded again with matching breath.
A scene in a noisy location may need replaced lines to keep the veteran's calm instructions clean.
A long story told across a table must be pristine, so any line spoiled on set is replaced.

terms.def: Sounds made in a studio, in sync with the picture, to replace or add the small noises of action: footsteps, cloth, a door, a cup set down.
terms.tanglish: Footsteps, dress rustle, door, cup: studio-la picture paathu, adhey neram-la sound ottirathu.

examples.note: The sound of paper moved across a desk during the reckoning is a Foley job, and it can say more than the music.
A cup set down and a chair moved are Foley sounds that fill a quiet film and make its silences audible.
Footsteps and the small sounds of procedure are Foley work, which carries information the dialogue refuses to state.
A glass set on a table during a telling is a Foley sound that gives each story its rhythm.

terms.def: Balancing dialogue, music, effects and ambience into one soundtrack so each is clear and the story is heard as intended. The final mix is done after picture lock.
terms.tanglish: Dialogue, music, effects, ambience ellaam balance panni oru soundtrack aakkuradhu. Picture lock-ku appuram.

examples.note: In the mix, the dean's calm line must sit above the room's noise so that the reckoning is heard before it is felt.
In the mix, music marks memory and then steps back, so the plain exchange at the end is heard alone.
In the mix, the sound design carries information the dialogue refuses to state, so its balance is part of the story.
In the mix, the voice of the teller must stay in front, because each story is told, not shown.

terms.def: Music and effects: a soundtrack with everything except dialogue, so that the film can be dubbed into other languages without redoing the sound.
terms.tanglish: Dialogue illama music + effects mattum thaniya oru track. Vera mozhi dubbing-ku.

examples.note: A clean M&E of a film that is largely spoken lets the comedy be re-voiced in another language without losing its sound world.
A film this quiet depends heavily on its small effects, so a good M&E carries most of its feeling into any dubbed version.
A film whose sound carries information needs its effects kept clean so a dubbed version still holds the same tension.
A film built on spoken stories will depend on the dubbing, with the M&E keeping its sound world constant under new voices.

terms.def: Digital Cinema Package: the standard folder of files that cinemas use to play a film, with the picture, sound and subtitles in an agreed format. Made at the end, from the finished film.
terms.tanglish: Cinema-la odaradhukku standard file package: picture, sound, subtitle. Padam mudinja piraku seiyyuvaanga.

examples.note: A cinema release needs a DCP made from the finished film, with the comic and reckoning scenes in exact picture and sound.
A cinema screening of a film that depends on silence needs a DCP made with care for the quietest sounds.
A theatrical release needs the film packaged for projection, with its dark rooms preserved on the big screen.
A theatrical release needs a DCP that keeps the voice of each story clear in a large room.

terms.def: Everything a distributor, festival or platform requires you to hand over when the film is finished: picture and sound masters, subtitles, trailer, posters, music and legal papers.
terms.tanglish: Padam mudinja piraku distributor / festival / platform kettaa kudukka vendiya ellaam: master, subtitle, trailer, poster, papers.

examples.note: A buyer for the film would ask for the finished picture and sound masters, subtitles, a trailer and the papers that prove the rights are clear.
A festival would ask for a screening copy, subtitles for any language not understood by the audience and stills for the programme.
A platform would ask for technical masters in an exact format, with subtitle files and the cleared music list.
A distributor would ask for a clean M&E and subtitles so the film can be sold in other languages.

terms.def: Whether a festival counts your film as new to its audience: world (first anywhere), international (first outside its home country), national or regional. Many festivals prefer or require a high status, so where it plays first matters.
terms.tanglish: Padam ippo thaan mudhal thadavai kaattura-nu festival eppadi eduthukkum: world / international / national / regional. Mudhal screening enga-nu mukkiyam.

examples.note: A film aimed at several festivals must decide where its first screening is, because an early local screening can cost it a higher status at a larger festival.
A small, personal film may hold out for a major festival's world premiere rather than spend it at a local one.
A genre film for a wider audience may start at a festival that welcomes thrillers, and then travel.
A film that expects a theatrical run needs to plan its festival dates around the release, because the order of screenings decides the status.

terms.def: Edits in which the sound and picture change at different moments. In a J-cut the next scene's sound starts before its picture; in an L-cut the previous scene's sound continues over the next picture.
terms.tanglish: Picture-um sound-um orey neram-la maaraadhu. J-cut: adutha scene sound munnaadi. L-cut: pazhaya scene sound adutha picture mela.

examples.note: A J-cut brings the sound of the next place in before the picture, so a comic scene can bleed into a consequence.
An L-cut lets a line from one scene carry over a close on the person who hears it in the next, binding the two moments.
A J-cut lets the sound of the next scene arrive early, building suspense without adding a shot.
An L-cut lets the teller's voice continue over the cop's face, putting the effect of the story in the same breath as the story.

terms.def: Existing music laid under a rough cut as a placeholder, to judge rhythm and mood. It is replaced by the real score, but it can mislead if you fall in love with it.
terms.tanglish: Rough cut-ku vera padam music podurathu, rhythm / mood paakka. Appuram original score vaarum.

examples.note: A temp track under the comic setup shows how much the scenes depend on music to sell the lie, before anyone writes a note.
A temp track under the reunion shows how far the film's restraint is helped or harmed by music, which is the main question of its score.
A temp track under the investigation shows whether the pace holds on its own or leans on music for tension.
A temp track under the tellings shows whether each story needs music or is stronger told plain.

terms.def: The original music composed for the film, laid to picture after the edit is locked. It tells the audience how to feel, so the best scores choose when not to.
terms.tanglish: Padathukkunnu compose panna music: edit lock aana piraku picture-kku match panni. Edhukku silent-aa irukkanum-nu therinjirukkanum.

examples.note: A score can sell the con in the early comic scenes, and then drop away so the reckoning is heard unaided.
A score here marks memory rather than instructing the audience how to feel about the present.
A score that stays out of the way lets sound design and silence carry the investigation's tension.
A score can give the stories a recurring sound, so a change in the tune signals a change in the form.

terms.def: A scene's length, counted in eighths of a page. A page is eight eighths, so a half-page scene is 4/8 and a scene that fills a page and a quarter is 10/8. Because one page of screenplay runs about a minute of screen time, eighths are how a schedule guesses how much of a day a scene will eat.
terms.tanglish: Oru page = 8 eighths. Paadhi page scene na 4/8. Scene evvalavu neelam-nu ethukku solra measure; adha vechchu thaan oru naal-la evvalavu scene edukka mudiyum-nu kanakku.

examples.note: A short comic exchange in a hallway may be 2/8 and a long confrontation in the dean's office may run over a page; the board uses those numbers to guess how many scenes make a realistic day.
A quiet night scene of two people talking could be 6/8 of a page, small on paper, but it still needs a whole night's patience, so eighths measure the script, not the effort.
A procedural scene that is only a few lines of dialogue can be 1/8, and it might still need a locked location and an evidence prop. Eighths count length, not difficulty.
A long interrogation scene might run several pages, so its eighths are large and the day it lands on needs fewer other scenes beside it.

terms.def: The running number a scene carries so everyone can refer to it. A new scene begins whenever the place or the time changes, which is exactly what a slugline announces. Numbers are usually frozen once the script is shared, so later additions get a letter (12A) instead of renumbering everything.
terms.tanglish: Ovvoru scene-kum oru number, ellarum adhaiye solluvaanga. Idam illa neram maarina pudhu scene. Script share panna piragu number maathaama, pudhusa vandhaa 12A maadhiri.

examples.note: A cut from the college hall to the same students outside in the corridor is a new scene because the place changed, so it gets its own number and its own row in the breakdown.
The same two people talking as the night moves on can be one scene or two: if the place and the unbroken time hold, it is one; if the story jumps ahead, it is two.
Returning to the same room the next morning is a new scene even though the set is the same, because the time moved, and the call sheet will name it by number.
A scene told again from another character's view is a new scene in the script, so it is numbered separately even if it shares a room with the one before.

terms.def: A heading under which a breakdown files one kind of need: cast, background actors, props, set dressing, wardrobe, hair and makeup, vehicles, animals, stunts, special effects, visual effects, special equipment. Every department reads only its own categories, so the list is the way the script becomes a set of separate shopping and planning lists.
terms.tanglish: Breakdown-la ovvoru thevaikkum oru category: cast, props, wardrobe, vehicles nu. Ovvoru department-um thanakku vendiyadha mattum paarthukkum.

examples.note: The corporate scenes would fill wardrobe and background rows while the campus scenes might lean on cast and crowd, so each department sees a different slice of the same script.
With very few extras and a handful of places, most of its weight falls on cast, wardrobe and the props of one evening.
Evidence, weapons and vehicles are separate categories, so the person who sources props is not wading through the stunt list.
Interrogation scenes load cast and props; chase or fight scenes load vehicles, stunts and special effects. The categories show which kind of day each scene is.

terms.def: The people who fill a scene without speaking lines: students in a corridor, customers in a shop, a crowd on a street. Also called extras. They are counted and costed apart from the cast, and a large crowd changes how long a scene takes.
terms.tanglish: Dialogue illaama scene-a nirappura aalunga: corridor-la students, kadai-la customers. Cast-ukku veru, kanakkum veru.

examples.note: A campus corridor or an office floor needs a dozen people who never speak, yet they are what makes those places look lived in, and they must be booked.
Two people in a mostly empty place need almost no background, which is a quiet saving the breakdown makes visible.
A busy station or street behind a conversation means background actors, a few more people to feed and to direct on the day.
A crowded public place changes the plan: the more background, the longer the setup, so the schedule gives such a scene extra time.

terms.def: Objects an actor handles or uses: a phone, a letter, a file, a weapon. If a person picks it up or uses it on screen, it is a prop. What merely sits in the room and is never touched is set dressing, and the two are budgeted and sourced by different people.
terms.tanglish: Actor kaiyila edukkura, use pannura, kadhaiyoda mukkiyamaana porul prop. Room-la summa irukkura porul set dressing.

examples.note: A certificate or mark sheet that changes hands is a prop, because the story depends on it being picked up and read.
An old photograph or a keepsake passed from one hand to another is a prop that must match from shot to shot.
A case file or piece of evidence held up to the camera is a prop; the shelves of files behind the desk are set dressing.
A gun on a table that someone reaches for is a prop; the other things on that table which nobody touches are dressing.

terms.def: The furniture, posters, curtains, clutter and other things that make a location look like somebody's place, which actors do not handle. Props are handled; set dressing is lived among. It belongs to production design, and a breakdown lists it separately so it is neither forgotten nor priced as a prop.
terms.tanglish: Location-a oru veedu maadhiri, office maadhiri kaattura furniture, poster, curtain. Actor thodaadhadhu. Production design paakkum.

examples.note: An office dressed with a heavy desk and framed photographs is set dressing, and it can say who holds power without an actor touching any of it.
A rented room made to feel like a place from twenty years ago is a job of dressing: the calendar, the bedspread, the cups on the shelf.
The cluttered walls of a station or a case room are dressing; the one item the officer lifts from the wall is a prop.
A bar or a room is dressed to match its character before the actors enter; the dressing sets the tone of the scene.

terms.def: Effects made physically on the set, in front of the camera: rain, smoke, a breakaway window, a controlled flame, a prop that explodes. Often abbreviated SFX. They happen on the day, need safety planning, and are not to be confused with visual effects, which are added digitally afterwards.
terms.tanglish: Set-la, camera munnaadiye nijamaa panra effects: mazhai, pugai, odayira kannaadi. Safety-um vendum. Post-la computer-la serkkardhu VFX, idhu SFX.

examples.note: A comic scene that needs rain or a smashed prop is SFX: it happens in front of the lens and must be rehearsed and made safe.
Rain on a window made with a sprinkler on the set is SFX; it is part of the shooting day, not something added later.
A smoke-filled room or a breakaway door in a raid scene is SFX, and the stunt team and the effects team plan it together.
A crash, a shattered window or a controlled spark in an action scene is done on the day, so it counts as SFX and needs time and safety.

terms.def: Effects created or altered digitally after the shoot, then composited into the picture: removing a wire, replacing a sky, adding a crowd, building a place that does not exist. Often abbreviated VFX. The difference from special effects is where it is made: on the set means SFX, on a computer after the shoot means VFX.
terms.tanglish: Shoot mudinjadhukku piragu computer-la serkkardhu: wire-a azhikkardhu, sky maathardhu. Idhu VFX. Set-la panna SFX.

examples.note: Extending a campus with a digital crowd or tidying a modern street of signs that do not belong would be VFX, planned in the breakdown but made in post.
Cleaning an unwanted modern object out of a period frame is VFX, and it is far cheaper if the shoot flags it on the day.
Removing a wire or hiding a rig after the fight is VFX; the shot is designed on set so that it can be cleaned later.
Painting out a safety wire or adding to a skyline after the shoot is VFX, and the effects supervisor has to be there on the day.

terms.def: Gear a scene needs beyond the ordinary kit: a crane, a drone, an underwater housing, a camera car, a rig for a long moving shot. A breakdown flags it so it is booked, paid for and given time, because it often adds a person or a permit as well.
terms.tanglish: Saadharana kit-ukku mela scene-ukku thevai: crane, drone, camera car. Munnaadiye book panna thaan mudiyum.

examples.note: A single big opening movement across a campus would flag a crane or a rig, and that scene needs setup time in the plan.
A restrained film may flag almost nothing, which is itself useful: the breakdown shows the equipment line stays short.
A moving shot through a building or along a street flags the rig that makes it possible, so it is booked before the day.
A camera car or a rig for a chase shot is special equipment, with a driver, a permit and extra time.

terms.def: An overhead map of a scene: the room as a plan, marks for where each actor stands and moves, and the camera positions and their moves drawn on it. It answers questions a shot list cannot, such as who crosses whom and where the lights and the crew can stand. With a storyboard and a shot list, it makes the plan for a scene.
terms.tanglish: Scene-a mela irundhu paarthaa maadhiri map: actor enga nikkaraanga, nagarraanga, camera enga. Storyboard-um shot list-um sernthu thaan oru scene plan.

examples.note: A two-person confrontation in an office is easier to plan from above: the desk, the door, the dean's chair and the protagonist's path across the floor.
The distance between two people on a bench or across a table, drawn from above, lets the crew see how far the camera may stand back.
A diagram of a room with several people shows who stands behind whom, and where the camera can go without a reflection or a shadow.
A table with two chairs and a door shows who can leave first, and tells the camera crew where they can stand.

terms.def: The creative and financial decision-makers whose deals are fixed before shooting: the writer, director, producers and principal cast. Their costs are largely agreed in advance and do not grow with the length of the shoot. The crew and equipment that follow are below the line.
terms.tanglish: Padam eduppadharkku munnaadiye deal mudikkura creative aalunga: writer, director, producer, mukkiya cast. Avanga selavu shoot neelatha poruthu maaradhu.

examples.note: The writer, director and lead cast form the fixed top of the budget; adding shoot days does not change what they were paid.
A film with two leads and a small crew keeps its above-the-line list short and its below-the-line list shorter still.
The writer-director and the lead actors are agreed upon first; the shoot days that follow are budgeted separately.
The leads and the director are on the top lines, agreed before cameras roll; the crew and the locations change with the schedule.

terms.def: Everything that is spent to make the film once the deals are fixed: crew, equipment, locations, sets, wardrobe, transport, food, insurance. Unlike the above-the-line costs, these tend to follow the shoot days, so a longer schedule usually means a larger below-the-line total.
terms.tanglish: Padam edukka selavaagura ellaam: crew, equipment, location, transport, saapaadu. Shoot naal koodinaa idhuvum koodum.

examples.note: Crew, campus locations, sets and transport rise with every extra shoot day; this is where a schedule overrun costs money.
A few locations and a small crew keep this part of the budget in check, and the days still set the total.
Crew, vehicles and locations for the case scenes go on these lines, and each added night adds to them.
Locations, permissions and crew for action scenes are billed by the day, so a rearranged schedule changes this total directly.

terms.def: The person who gets the film made: finds the money, hires the key people, protects the deal and the delivery. A producer decides whether the film goes ahead, what it may cost and when it must be done, and then leaves the day-to-day running of the set to others.
terms.tanglish: Padam nadakka paakkaravar: panam, key aalunga, deal, delivery. Set-a day-to-day paakkardhu veru aalunga.

examples.note: A film whose hero needs a corporate world and a campus depends on a producer who commits the funds for both before anyone books a location.
On a small film the producer may also be the person calling the cast and hiring the hall, which is why it is the title that gets doubled up.
A film built on locations and evidence needs a producer who has secured the permissions, so the shoot can start on time.
Large action days need a producer who has agreed the budget with the director, so that the schedule is the plan both of them accept.

terms.def: The person who turns the budget into a working plan and keeps spending to it: crew deals, schedule checks, daily costs. In many industries the unit production manager does a similar job. The line producer answers to the producer and works closely with the first assistant director, who owns the day's schedule on set.
terms.tanglish: Budget-a plan-aa maathi selavu paakkaravar. Producer-ukku answer pannuvaar, 1st AD-oda sernthu velai. Set-la naal schedule AD-udaiyadhu.

examples.note: A schedule with a big crowd day and a small drama day is checked by the line producer against the money, before it goes to the AD.
A film shot in a few nights has a light line-producing job: a small crew list, a short call sheet and the daily cost.
A film with many locations needs a line producer who sees that the schedule does not hop across the city and burn travel time.
When an action day overruns, it is the line producer who counts what the extra hours cost and what can move.

terms.def: One day of shooting, and the unit in which a schedule and a budget meet. Crew, locations, equipment and food are mostly paid by the day, so a script change saves money only if it removes a whole day. Shortening a scene by a few lines usually saves nothing; moving or removing the last scene on a day can save the day.
terms.tanglish: Shoot-oda oru naal; schedule-um budget-um sandhikkura alavu. Oru scene-a kuraichaalum, mulu naal midhikkaadha varai selavu kuraiyaadhu.

examples.note: Cutting a short comic scene from a crowded day saves little; cutting the only scene that needs the campus on a separate day saves the whole day.
With a handful of nights, each night is a large share of the money, so removing one scene helps only if it frees the whole night.
A day of three procedural scenes in one room costs the same whether one of them is shortened or not; removing all three frees the day.
Because the schedule groups scenes by location, dropping one of several scenes that need the same set may free nothing.

terms.def: Sending camera footage to a shared online store while the shoot is still going on, usually as small copies, so that editors, the director and others can start work the same day. It does not replace safely copying the original files on set; it is an early, light copy.
terms.tanglish: Shoot nadakkumbodhe footage-a online-la anuppardhu, sinna copies-a, edit pannuravanga appove aarambikka. Original file copy set-la thaan irukkanum.

examples.note: A comic scene shot in the morning can reach the editor by evening, so he can see whether the timing works while the set is still standing.
A night shoot gets its footage to the editor before the sun is up, which means a weak take is noticed in time for a pick-up.
Procedural footage reaching the editor the same day shows if all the information made it into frame, while reshoots are still easy.
Fight and chase footage can be checked for continuity on the same day, while the stunt team is still on the schedule.

terms.def: A small, light copy of a camera file made so that it can be edited on an ordinary computer or sent online quickly. The edit is made on proxies; at the end the project is pointed back at the full-resolution originals for finishing. The proxy is only a stand-in, never the master.
terms.tanglish: Camera file-oda sinna, light copy, normal computer-la edit pannalaam. Mudivula original file-ukku thirumba point pannuvom.

examples.note: The editor can work on a laptop with small copies of the comic scenes, then relink to the original files when the cut is locked.
Soft night footage is cut from small copies, and the grade is made on the originals so that the dark detail is not lost.
Long procedural takes cut easily from proxies, and the original files wait safely on the backup drives.
Action shots cut from proxies play smoothly on a laptop, and the conform later restores the full quality.

terms.def: A rule for keeping footage safe: three copies of the data, on two different kinds of storage, with one copy kept in a different place. Footage from a shoot day cannot be reshot cheaply, so no card is wiped until every copy has been checked.
terms.tanglish: Moonu copy, rendu vagai storage, onnu veru idathula. Camera card-a copy check pannaama azhikka koodaadhu.

examples.note: Even a comic scene with a big crowd cannot be reshot on a whim, so the day's cards are copied three times before anyone formats them.
The night's footage is the only record of a night that will not come again; it goes to three places before the cards are cleared.
Case-scene footage is copied to a hard drive and to a second kind of storage on set, and a third copy goes to another place before the unit leaves.
A day of action cannot be restaged cheaply; each card is copied, checked and stored in three places before it is reused.

terms.def: A short fingerprint calculated from a file's contents. Calculate it before and after a copy; if the two match, the copy is identical, bit for bit, and if they differ the copy is damaged. It is how a data person proves a card was copied correctly before the card is cleared.
terms.tanglish: File-oda fingerprint maadhiri oru short code. Copy-ukku munnaadiyum pinnaadiyum ondrunaa copy sari; maaritchuna copy kedu.

examples.note: After copying the crowd day, the DIT compares the fingerprints to know every file arrived whole before the cards are reused.
A single corrupted file from the night's card would be noticed at once, because its fingerprint would not match.
The DIT checks that each case-scene file copied exactly, so nothing is missing when the editor opens the folder.
Large action files are the likeliest to fail in a copy, so each one is matched against its fingerprint before it is trusted.
